questionTypes.label: True / False / Not Given
questionTypes.description: Decide if statements match the passage information
strategy: Read the statement FIRST, then scan the passage for the relevant section
TRUE = the passage says exactly this (maybe in different words)
FALSE = the passage says the OPPOSITE of this
NOT GIVEN = the passage doesn't mention this at all — don't use your own knowledge
Beware of qualifiers: 'all', 'some', 'never', 'always' — they change meaning completely
Statements follow the order of the passage — use this to locate answers faster
commonTraps: A topic is mentioned but the SPECIFIC claim isn't — that's NOT GIVEN, not TRUE
Your own opinion agrees with the statement, but the passage doesn't say it — NOT GIVEN
The passage uses similar words but means something different — read carefully
Absolute words like 'always' or 'never' are often FALSE

example.passage: Research shows that bilingual children often develop stronger problem-solving skills than monolingual peers. However, the age at which a second language is introduced may influence outcomes.
example.statement: Bilingual children always perform better academically than monolingual children.
example.explanation: The passage mentions problem-solving skills, not academic performance in general. 'Always' is also an absolute not supported by 'often'.

questionTypes.label: Yes / No / Not Given
questionTypes.description: Identify the writer's views and claims
strategy: Similar to T/F/NG but focuses on the WRITER'S OPINION, not facts
YES = the writer agrees with this / claims this
NO = the writer disagrees with this / contradicts this
NOT GIVEN = the writer doesn't express a view on this
Look for opinion language: 'I believe', 'it is clear that', 'arguably', 'should'
The writer's view may be implied through word choice, not stated directly
commonTraps: The passage presents someone else's opinion — that's not necessarily the WRITER'S view
The writer mentions a topic but doesn't give their opinion — NOT GIVEN
Hedging language ('may', 'might', 'could') makes the view weaker, not absent

example.passage: While some argue that homework is essential, I believe the evidence suggests that excessive homework does more harm than good for primary school children.
example.statement: The writer thinks homework is always harmful.
example.explanation: The writer says 'excessive' homework is harmful for 'primary school' children — not ALL homework for ALL students.

questionTypes.label: Matching Headings
questionTypes.description: Choose the best heading for each paragraph
strategy: Read ALL the headings first — understand the options before reading paragraphs
Read the FIRST and LAST sentence of each paragraph — they usually contain the main idea
Cross out headings as you use them (each heading is used once)
Don't match based on a single word — match the MAIN IDEA of the whole paragraph
Do the easiest paragraphs first, then eliminate options for harder ones
Look for paraphrasing — the heading won't use the same words as the paragraph
commonTraps: A heading contains a word from the paragraph but doesn't capture the main idea
Two headings seem to fit — pick the one that covers the WHOLE paragraph, not just one sentence
The paragraph has a topic sentence buried in the middle, not at the start

questionTypes.label: Matching Information
questionTypes.description: Match statements to the paragraph they appear in
strategy: Read all statements first and underline key words
Scan each paragraph for the specific information in each statement
A paragraph may be used more than once — read the instructions carefully
Look for paraphrased versions of the statement's key ideas
This is a scanning exercise — don't read every word, scan for key terms
commonTraps: The same topic appears in multiple paragraphs — make sure the SPECIFIC information matches
Similar vocabulary in different paragraphs can mislead you

questionTypes.label: Sentence / Summary Completion
questionTypes.description: Fill gaps using words from the passage or a word list
strategy: Check the word limit — 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS' means 1 or 2, not 3
The answer must be grammatically correct in the sentence
Copy words EXACTLY from the passage — don't change the form
Read the sentence before and after the blank to understand context
Answers usually follow passage order
If given a word list, eliminate options as you use them
commonTraps: Writing 3 words when the limit is 2 — always check the instruction
Changing the word form (e.g., writing 'developed' when the passage says 'development')
Spelling mistakes count — copy carefully
Including articles (a/the) unnecessarily — they count towards the word limit

example.passage: The project, which was funded by the National Science Foundation, aimed to develop affordable solar panels for rural communities.
example.statement: The project received funding from the _______.
example.explanation: Copy the exact phrase. It fits grammatically and within word limits.

questionTypes.label: Multiple Choice
questionTypes.description: Choose the correct answer from 4 options
strategy: Read the question stem carefully — understand what it's asking
Try to think of the answer BEFORE looking at options
Eliminate obviously wrong answers first
Beware of options that are TRUE but don't answer the specific question
The correct answer paraphrases the passage — it rarely uses the exact same words
'All of the above' and 'None of the above' are rare in IELTS
commonTraps: An option contains exact words from the passage but misrepresents the meaning
An option is true in real life but not stated in the passage
Two options seem correct — re-read the question to see which one is MORE accurate

questionTypes.label: Matching Features / Names
questionTypes.description: Match statements to people, dates, or categories
strategy: Scan for names/dates/categories first — they're easy to spot
Read what each person says or what each date represents
Multiple statements can match the same person/feature
Look for reporting verbs: 'argues', 'suggests', 'found that', 'believes'
commonTraps: Confusing what person A said about person B's research with person B's own views
A name appears multiple times — make sure you match the RIGHT statement to the RIGHT mention

questionTypes.label: Short Answer Questions
questionTypes.description: Answer questions using words from the passage
strategy: Read the question and identify key words to scan for
Answers follow passage order
Stick to the word limit — check the instructions
Use exact words from the passage, not your own words
Question words tell you what to look for: 'when' = date/time, 'where' = place, 'who' = person
commonTraps: Giving a full sentence answer when they want 1-3 words
Answering with information from the wrong part of the passage

skimmingTips: Read the title, subtitle, and any headings first — they tell you the topic and structure
Read the first sentence of each paragraph to get the main idea
Don't read every word — move your eyes across the text quickly
Look for topic sentences (usually first or last in a paragraph)
Skip examples and details on first read — you'll come back for them
Aim to skim the entire passage in 2-3 minutes before answering questions
scanningTips: Know WHAT you're looking for before you scan
Look for capital letters (names, places), numbers, dates, and italics
Move your finger down the page to guide your eyes
Don't read — just look for the specific word or synonym
Once you find the area, slow down and read carefully around it
Practice scanning newspaper articles daily to build speed

recommended.tip: Dense academic text — allocate extra time

tips: If stuck on a question for more than 90 seconds, move on and come back
NEVER leave a question blank — guess if you must (no penalty for wrong answers)
Transfer answers to the answer sheet as you go, not at the end
Spend 2-3 minutes skimming each passage before answering
